node.label: Ranajit Guha
node.date_label: A Rule of Property for Bengal 1963 · “On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India” 1982 · Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency 1983 · “The Prose of Counter-Insurgency” 1983 · “Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography” 1989 (book 1997)
node.description: A historian of colonial India, who taught at Sussex and the Australian National University and edited Subaltern Studies from its first volume (1982) until he left the editorial team in 1988. The opening statement holds that the historiography of Indian nationalism 'has for a long time been dominated by elitism—colonialist elitism and bourgeois-nationalist elitism', and that it leaves out 'the politics of the people', 'an autonomous domain' that 'neither originated from elite politics nor did its existence depend on the latter', while allowing 'a great deal of overlap' between the two (1982). Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency (1983) attributes 'a consciousness' to the rebel peasant, holds that Hobsbawm's 'pre-political' 'helps little in understanding the experience of colonial India', and reads that consciousness through the records of counter-insurgency; 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency' (1983) finds colonial, nationalist and radical histories alike making the rebel 'only a contingent element in another history with another subject'. 'Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography' (1989; book 1997) defines hegemony, against 'the Gramscian juxtaposition of domination and hegemony', as dominance in which 'Persuasion (P) outweighs Coercion (C)', and argues that colonial dominance had 'quite erroneously been endowed with hegemony'. In period, Spivak (1985) read the recovery of subaltern consciousness as 'a strategic use of positivist essentialism', O'Hanlon (1988) found 'the classic figure of Western humanism' readmitted 'in the figure of the subaltern himself', Bayly (1988) found that the approach sometimes seemed to postulate an 'unchanging peasantry', and Sarkar (1997) an 'unnoticed drift' towards nationalist positions 'even in Guha's initial formulation of the project'.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Ranajit Guha (1923–2023); A Rule of Property for Bengal: An Essay on the Idea of Permanent Settlement (Paris: Mouton, 1963); Preface and “On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India”, Subaltern Studies I (1982); Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India (Delhi, 1983); “The Prose of Counter-Insurgency”, Subaltern Studies II (1983); “Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography”, Subaltern Studies VI (1989), and Dominance without Hegemony: History and Power in Colonial India (1997); Selected Subaltern Studies, edited with Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak (1988). Readings: Spivak (1985); O'Hanlon (1988); Bayly (1988); Sarkar (1997); Chakrabarty (2000).
node.scope_note: This entry rests on texts read on 2026-10-14: the Subaltern Studies I preface and opening statement in the Selected Subaltern Studies reprint (1988, pp. 35–44); the introduction of Elementary Aspects (pp. 1–17), its bibliography and pp. 89–90; 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency' (Subaltern Studies II, 1983, pp. 1–42) in full; and 'Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography' (Subaltern Studies VI, 1989), pp. 210–215, 227–233, 276–277, 291–292 and 299–303. The 1963 and 1997 books are known here only from metadata and from later quotation; the rest of Elementary Aspects and of the 1989 essay is unread. He is not presented as the founder of a field. In period, Chakrabarty called him 'the founder of the group' (1997) and James C. Scott wrote that Elementary Aspects 'became, in effect, the founding document' of 'the Subaltern Studies School', while finding 'school' too rigid a term (1999); his own 1982 statement claims 'no more than to try and indicate an orientation'. Contested in period by Spivak (1985, a reading from within the project), O'Hanlon (1988), Bayly (1988) and Sarkar (1997); Javeed Alam's Marxist critique (Social Scientist, 1983) is known only through O'Hanlon and is unread. Vinay Bahl (1997) is unread. Chakrabarty's 2000 account of the project is a member's later reading and carries no edge alone. Not Ramachandra Guha, the environmental historian, who has a separate people record.

proposed_edges.relationship: The programme statement of Subaltern Studies: a critique of colonialist and bourgeois-nationalist elitism, an autonomous but overlapping domain of 'the politics of the people', and a method of reading rebel consciousness through counter-insurgency records (1982–83)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. Preface to Subaltern Studies I (dated Canberra, August 1981), read in the Selected Subaltern Studies reprint (Oxford, 1988), p. 35: the series is to 'rectify the elitist bias characteristic of much research and academic work' in South Asian studies; 'subaltern' is taken in the Concise Oxford sense, 'of inferior rank', as 'a name for the general attribute of subordination in South Asian society whether this is expressed in terms of class, caste, age, gender and office or in any other way'. 'On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India' (same reprint, pp. 37–44; Subaltern Studies I pagination is pp. 1–8): elitist historiography 'is of course not without its uses' (p. 38) but 'fails to acknowledge, far less interpret, the contribution made by the people on their own, that is, independently of the elite' (p. 39); 'What clearly is left out of this un-historical historiography is the politics of the people', 'an autonomous domain, for it neither originated from elite politics nor did its existence depend on the latter', 'As modern as indigenous elite politics' (p. 40); the two domains were not 'hermetically sealed off'; 'there was a great deal of overlap' (p. 42); the same class 'dominant in one area ... could be among the dominated in another' (p. 44). He claims a direction, not a doctrine: 'Let a hundred flowers blossom and we don't mind even the weeds' (p. 43); 'We claim no more than to try and indicate an orientation' (p. 43). Method, Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency (1983), introduction read (Duke 1999 printing, which keeps the 1983 Oxford pagination): 'To acknowledge the peasant as the maker of his own rebellion is to attribute ... a consciousness to him' (p. 4); 'How then are we to get in touch with the consciousness of insurgency when our access to it is barred thus by the discourse of counter-insurgency?'; 'It should be possible therefore to read the presence of a rebel consciousness as a necessary and pervasive element within that body of evidence' (p. 15). 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency', Subaltern Studies II (Delhi, 1983), pp. 1–42, read in full: historiography takes the peasant rebel 'merely as an empirical person or member of a class, but not as an entity whose will and reason constituted the praxis called rebellion' (p. 2); 'Cause is made to stand in as a phantom surrogate for Reason' (p. 3); the historian should 'stop pretending that it can fully grasp a past consciousness and reconstitute it' (p. 33). In-period reception, a member's reading first: Spivak, 'Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography', Subaltern Studies IV (Delhi, 1985), pp. 330–363 (read): the group 'offers a theory of change' (p. 330); its practice is 'closer to deconstruction' (p. 332) and its presuppositions are 'not, strictly speaking, consonant with a desire to find a consciousness (here of the subaltern) in a positive and pure state' (p. 333); quoting Elementary Aspects p. 15, she reads 'the project to retrieve the subaltern consciousness' 'as a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest' (pp. 341–342), which 'would get the group off the dangerous hook of claiming to establish the truth-knowledge of the subaltern and his consciousness' (p. 356); 'The group is scrupulous in its consideration towards women' but overlooks 'how important the concept-metaphor woman is' (p. 356). Rosalind O'Hanlon, 'Recovering the Subject' (Modern Asian Studies 22:1, 1988, pp. 189–224; read in the Verso reprint, 2000, pp. 72–115, whose pages are cited): 'the classic figure of Western humanism—the self-originating, self-determining individual ... is readmitted through the back door in the figure of the subaltern himself' (p. 74). C. A. Bayly, 'Rallying Around the Subaltern' (Journal of Peasant Studies 16:1, 1988, pp. 110–120; Verso reprint pp. 116–126): the Subalterns 'acted mainly as a catalyst' for an existing minority interest (p. 116); Guha's approach 'seems sometimes to postulate the existence of an unchanging peasantry and unified peasant consciousness defined by struggle with colonialism' (p. 121). Sumit Sarkar, 'The Decline of the Subaltern in Subaltern Studies' (1997; pp. 82–87 and 90–94 read, pp. 84–87 against the page images): the early volumes were 'largely ignored in the West' while debated in 'Left-leaning intellectual circles in India' (p. 84); 'it was argued with considerable justice by Guha and other contributors' that anti-colonial movements had been explained 'far too often' by economic pressures and mobilization from the top (p. 85); the claims of a new 'paradigm' 'were certainly over-flamboyant' (p. 86); the theoretical turn 'had its origins in Guha's attempt to use some of the language and methods of Lévi-Straussian structuralism' (p. 87). Founder language is attributed, not adopted: Chakrabarty (1997) calls him 'the founder of the group' (subaltern source); Scott's foreword to the 1999 Duke printing writes that Elementary Aspects 'became, in effect, the founding document of what is now known as the Subaltern Studies School', adding that 'The term school conveys far too much in the way of a rigid orthodoxy' (p. ix). Later reading, labelled: Chakrabarty (Nepantla, 2000) treats 'the work of the historian Ranajit Guha in the period when he acted as the founding editor' as 'the founding texts of the project' (p. 11). edge_115 (subaltern → post) and edge_159 (gramsci → subaltern) stay.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: popular_politics ('Popular politics and elite historiography'; 'Autonomy is an argued distinction, with interaction and regional variation built into the early statement'; works Guha 1982 and Elementary Aspects 1983) holds him alone and matches the checked texts, including the overlap and regional-variation qualifications (pp. 42, 44). The strand's works field could add 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency' (1983) at release.

proposed_edges.relationship: Colonialist and bourgeois-nationalist histories of India criticised as two forms of elitism that write nationalism as 'a sort of spiritual biography of the Indian elite' and leave out popular initiative (1982), extended to the shared liberal assumption that colonial dominance was hegemonic (1989)
proposed_edges.map_label: Against elitist histories of Indian nationalism, 1982–89
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. 'On Some Aspects of the Historiography of Colonial India' (1982; Selected Subaltern Studies reprint, 1988, pp. 37–44, read): 'The historiography of Indian nationalism has for a long time been dominated by elitism—colonialist elitism and bourgeois-nationalist elitism'; both 'share the prejudice that the making of the Indian nation and the development of the consciousness—nationalism—which informed this process were exclusively or predominantly elite achievements' (p. 37). The colonialist kind treats nationalism as 'a sort of “learning process”' driven by 'the expectation of rewards' (p. 38); the nationalist kind writes it up 'as a sort of spiritual biography of the Indian elite' (p. 38). Neither can explain 'the anti-Rowlatt upsurge of 1919 and the Quit India movement of 1942' as 'popular initiative asserting itself ... in defiance or absence of elite control' (p. 39). The qualification he keeps: 'Elitist historiography is of course not without its uses' (p. 38), and 'even the elitists have a part to play if only by way of teaching by negative examples' (p. 43). 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency' (Subaltern Studies II, 1983, read): in bourgeois-nationalist historiography 'it is an elite consciousness which is read into all peasant movements as their motive force', producing 'such grotesqueries as the characterization of the Indigo Rebellion of 1860 as “the first non-violent mass movement”' (p. 38). 'Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography' (Subaltern Studies VI, 1989, pp. 210–309; pp. 210–215, 227–233, 291–292 and 299–303 read): 'There was one Indian battle that Britain never won. It was a battle for appropriation of the Indian past' (p. 210); 'History became thus a game for two to play as the alien colonialist project of appropriation was matched by an indigenous nationalist project of counter-appropriation' (p. 212); both rest on 'a fundamental agreement between the Indian bourgeoisie and the British' from 'the standpoint of liberalism' (p. 212); 'dominance under colonial conditions has quite erroneously been endowed with hegemony' (p. 228). On the Cambridge historians: 'The subject of this neo-colonialist historiography is the Empire' (p. 292); Anil Seal's 'general explanation' is 'a kind of academic confidence trick' (p. 300). In-period criticism of the stance: Sarkar (1997, p. 92, read) sees 'an unnoticed drift implicit even in Guha's initial formulation of the project in Subaltern Studies I': 'The “historiography of colonial India” somehow slides quickly into that of Indian nationalism', and the central problematic 'ultimately becomes “the historic failure of the nation to come into its own”' (quoting Subaltern Studies I, pp. 2–3, 7). Later reading, labelled: Chakrabarty (2000, p. 14) describes the series as starting 'as a critique of two contending schools of history: the Cambridge school and that of the nationalist historians'. This edge carries the story now told by edge_604 (subaltern → nationaltradition), whose relabel is proposed; edge_114 (subaltern → anticolonial) is discussed under edge_revisions.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: national_exclusions ('Nationalist exclusions and alternative scales'; 'Guha and Chatterjee question elite and modular national accounts') holds him with Chatterjee and Ogot and matches the checked 1982 argument.

proposed_edges.relationship: Peasant insurgency in colonial India read as deliberate political action against a composite dominance of landlord, moneylender and state, whose limits define 'the quality of that politics' rather than denying it (1983)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India (1983), introduction pp. 1–17 read (Duke 1999 printing; 1983 Oxford pagination, checked against the Delhi edition's text): 'Insurgency was thus the necessary antithesis of colonialism' (p. 2); the first histories of revolt were 'a discourse of power' (p. 3). Spontaneity is rejected as 'an idea that is elitist as well as erroneous' (p. 4). For colonial India, 'there was nothing in the militant movements of its rural masses that was not political' (p. 6), because 'the hitherto discrete powers of the landlord, the moneylender and the official came to form, under colonial rule, a composite apparatus of dominance over the peasant', a subjection 'primarily political in character' (p. 8). 'There was nothing spontaneous about all this in the sense of being unthinking and wanting in deliberation'; 'insurgency affirmed its political character precisely by its negative and inversive procedure' (p. 9). He keeps the limits: rebel aims that failed 'to rise above localism, sectarianism and ethnicity' do 'not take away from the essentially political character of their activity but defines the quality of that politics by specifying its limitations' (p. 10); 'It would be wrong of course to overestimate the maturity of this politics' (p. 10); it was 'a somewhat inchoate and naive state of consciousness' (p. 11). In-period criticism: O'Hanlon (1988; Verso reprint, 2000) sets his book apart from cruder 'literal' readings of autonomy ('I want to distinguish Ranajit Guha's work in the book Elementary Aspects', p. 85), yet, following Dipankar Gupta, finds the 'culturological' style 'carried to an extreme' there, so that 'the failure of peasant movements to spread' is explained by a 'habit of thinking and acting on a small and local scale' rather than by structural features (pp. 86–87); she sees 'his forceful insistence upon humanism's unitary subject-agent in its most extreme form' (p. 89). Sarkar (1997) writes that Guha's analyses of rumour, crime and insurgency 'were appreciated by many who could not accept the overall framework of Elementary Aspects' (p. 86). Later reading, labelled: Chakrabarty (2000) calls the redefinition of 'the political' 'the critical theoretical break' (p. 15). The related critique of Hobsbawm's 'pre-political' is edge 4. edge_357 (subaltern → political) tells the same story under Guha's name; its relabel is proposed.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: popular_radicalism ('Radical ideas and popular political action'; 'Compare religious radicalism, Chartist participation and colonial peasant insurgency without making one a derivative instance of another') holds him with Hill and Dorothy Thompson and matches the checked introduction.

proposed_edges.relationship: Hobsbawm's category 'pre-political', credited as pioneering, judged to help 'little in understanding the experience of colonial India', where peasant militancy was political (1983)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own text. Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency in Colonial India (1983), introduction pp. 5–6 read (Duke 1999 printing; 1983 Oxford pagination): those who identify consciousness with organization and politics can call mass activity 'unconscious, hence pre-political' (p. 5). 'The image of the pre-political peasant rebel in societies still to be fully industrialized owes a great deal to E. J. Hobsbawm's pioneering work published over two decades ago'; Hobsbawm 'uses this term again and again to describe a state of supposedly absolute or near absence of political consciousness or organization' (p. 5). Hobsbawm's words as Guha quotes them: 'the social brigand appears ... only before the poor have reached political consciousness or acquired more effective methods of social agitation'; 'The bandit is a pre-political phenomenon and his strength is in inverse proportion to that of organized revolutionism and Socialism or Communism'; 'traditional forms of peasant discontent' were 'virtually devoid of any explicit ideology, organization or programme'; 'pre-political people' are those 'who have not yet found, or only begun to find, a specific language in which to express their aspirations about the world' (pp. 5–6). His note cites 'Hobsbawm: 2, 5, 13, 23, 96, 118' and Hobsbawm and Rudé's Captain Swing (pp. 19, 205); his bibliography lists Primitive Rebels (Manchester, 1959) and Captain Swing (London, 1969). He grants the European case and notes an inconsistency: 'Hobsbawm's material is of course derived almost entirely from the European experience and his generalizations are perhaps in accord with it, although one detects a certain contradiction' between banditry having 'next to no organization or ideology' and being 'a rather primitive form of organized social protest' (p. 6). Then: 'Whatever its validity for other countries the notion of pre-political peasant insurgency helps little in understanding the experience of colonial India. For there was nothing in the militant movements of its rural masses that was not political' (p. 6). Elsewhere the book credits 'E. J. Hobsbawm's pioneering formulation of the concept of “social banditry”' (p. 90, read in the 1983 Delhi edition's text). Hobsbawm's words are given only as Guha quotes them; Primitive Rebels was not read. Guha's quotation has 'express their aspirations about the world', the wording the 1.132 review reported from an OCR witness of Primitive Rebels p. 2, where Chakrabarty (2000, Provincializing Europe p. 12) has 'express themselves'; Chakrabarty's Nepantla essay (2000, p. 16) also quotes 'aspirations', citing Hobsbawm (1978, 2). This gives a second, earlier quoted-in witness for the edge_917 wording question, not a reading of Hobsbawm. Reception: Chakrabarty credits the critique to Guha in Provincializing Europe (2000, p. 11; post source) and writes that rejecting the category 'fundamentally pluralizes the history of power in global modernity' (Nepantla, 2000, p. 19). No reply by Hobsbawm was looked for or read. This edge is the origin edge_917 (dipesh_chakrabarty → eric_hobsbawm) names ('the critique Guha began (1983)').
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The eric_hobsbawm person entry has no strands. As with edge_917, the critique concerns the category 'pre-political', which no strand maps.
proposed_edges.include_note: Person-to-person critique in Guha's own words (precedents: edge_917, edge_310). The Hobsbawm text should still be checked in a printed or page-image copy of Primitive Rebels (1959), pp. 2–5, before any of the quoted wording is attributed to Hobsbawm directly.

proposed_edges.relationship: Thompson's account of the rule of law as 'a cultural achievement of universal significance' (Whigs and Hunters, 1975) rejected from colonial India, where bourgeois culture 'hits its historical limit', after drawing on the same book for comparisons with peasant crime (1983–89)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own text. 'Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography', Subaltern Studies VI (Delhi, 1989), pp. 276–277 read (Digital Library of India scan of the volume): asking 'What rule of law' existed under the Raj (p. 276), he finds the answer in 'the pervasive power of the ideology of law in English political thought', which assumed 'the status of “a cultural achievement of universal significance” in the eyes not only of English liberals and colonialists like Dodwell, but also, alas, of English radicals like E. P. Thompson from whom those words are taken' (p. 277). 'Neither the special pleading by Dodwell ... nor the ingenuity of Thompson when he tries unsuccessfully to disentangle himself from the metaphysical implications of his statement by allowing for the class manipulation of the rule of law, can take away from the fact that bourgeois culture hits its historical limit in colonialism' (p. 277). His notes cite Whigs and Hunters (London, 1975), p. 265, and pp. 258–69, especially 265–7. Whigs and Hunters was not read for this draft; the phrase is taken as Guha quotes it. The critique follows earlier use: Elementary Aspects (1983) draws on Thompson's account of the Blacks, the authorities' 'one common blur' of 'outrages by the Blacks' (p. 89) and the Blacks as an intermediate type between 'social bandits' and 'agrarian rebels' (p. 90), read in the 1983 Delhi edition's text. In-period context: Sarkar (1997, p. 83, read) writes that among historiographical influences on Subaltern Studies 'that of British Marxian social history was probably the most significant', that 'Ranajit Guha seems to have often used “subaltern” somewhat in the way Thompson deployed the term “plebeian”', and (n. 3) that Elementary Aspects 'frequently cited Thompson with approval', to Whigs and Hunters and Albion's Fatal Tree. The edge therefore records a dispute over one claim, not a rejection of Thompson. No reply by Thompson was looked for. edge_083 (marx → subaltern, Thompson's reception) stays.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: The ep_thompson person entry has no strands. A reviewer could note Whigs and Hunters (1975) in its works.
proposed_edges.include_note: Person-to-person critique in Guha's own words. The influence direction (Thompson → Guha) is recorded here as context and in edges_considered_not_proposed, not drawn as a second arrow.

proposed_edges.relationship: Gramsci's notes on subaltern groups, spontaneity and the 'first elements' of politics frame the founding preface and Elementary Aspects (1982–83); hegemony is later redefined against 'the Gramscian juxtaposition of domination and hegemony' (1989)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: His own in-period statements. Preface to Subaltern Studies I (1982; Selected Subaltern Studies reprint, p. 35, read): the series cannot 'even remotely match the six-point project envisaged by Antonio Gramsci in his “Notes on Italian History”'; subordination is 'one of the constitutive terms in a binary relationship of which the other is dominance, for “subaltern groups are always subject to the activity of ruling groups, even when they rebel and rise up”'. The quoted words are Gramsci's (Selections from the Prison Notebooks, 1971, p. 55, checked in the gramsci source; the preface does not name the source). Elementary Aspects (1983), introduction read: the critique of 'pure spontaneity' follows 'Antonio Gramsci whose words are quoted above' ('there is no room for pure spontaneity in history', p. 5), with the quoted passage on a 'scholastic and academic historico-political outlook' (p. 4) taken from 'Spontaneity and Conscious Leadership' (n., Gramsci: 196–200); leadership is described 'in Gramsci's words, as “multiple elements of 'conscious leadership' but no one of them ... predominant”' (p. 10); and the book's title concept comes from the 'first elements' which Gramsci called 'the pillars of politics and of any collective action whatsoever' (p. 12, citing Gramsci: 144; the passage, 'Elements of Politics', checked at Selections p. 144). 'Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography' (1989, pp. 231–232, read): 'As used in this essay, hegemony stands for a condition of Dominance (D), such that, in the organic composition of the latter, Persuasion (P) outweighs Coercion (C)'; this 'avoids the Gramscian juxtaposition of domination and hegemony (a term sometimes used in the Prison Notebooks synonymously with leadership) as antinomies, which has, alas, provided too often a theoretical pretext for the fabrication of a liberal absurdity—the absurdity of the idea of an uncoercive state—in spite of the basic drive of Gramsci's own work to the contrary'. The same definition is quoted from the 1997 book, p. 23, in Spivak's 'The New Subaltern' (Verso, 2000, n. 3), a later quoted-in witness. In-period readings: Sarkar (1997, p. 82) notes 'evocations of Gramsci' in Guha's 1982 preface and essay; O'Hanlon (1988; Verso reprint p. 102) finds 'no concerted attempt to construct a theory of domination as hegemony, as the invocation of Gramsci might have led us to expect', and agrees with Suneet Chopra and Javeed Alam 'that the series has not turned out to be a Gramscian project at all' (Alam and Chopra unread). Wikidata Q475026 states 'influenced by' Antonio Gramsci (P737); this is recorded as a Wikidata statement, not evidence. edge_159 (gramsci → subaltern) stays for the collective adaptation (for example David Arnold's 'Gramsci and Peasant Subalternity in India', reprinted in Mapping Subaltern Studies, 2000, ch. 3; not read); edge_159's evidence note names Guha, and a reviewer may trim that clause.
proposed_edges.target_strand_note: Target is a person entry without strands.

proposed_edges.relationship: Guha's critique of the 'pre-political' and his founding statements for Subaltern Studies, which Chakrabarty names as the starting point of his own argument for provincializing Europe (1997–2000)
proposed_edges.map_label: From Guha's critique of the 'pre-political' to provincializing Europe, 1983–2000
proposed_edges.evidence_note: In Chakrabarty's own in-period words. 'Minority Histories, Subaltern Pasts' (Perspectives, AHA, November 1997; subaltern source, read for 1.132) calls Guha 'the founder of the group'. Provincializing Europe (2000), introduction (post source, read for 1.132): Subaltern Studies registered 'a deep sense of unease with the very idea of the “political”', 'Nowhere ... more visible than in Ranajit Guha's criticism of the British historian Eric Hobsbawm's category “prepolitical” in his 1983 book Elementary Aspects of Peasant Insurgency' (p. 11); Guha's critique 'fundamentally pluralizes the history of power in global modernity' (p. 14); 'My argument for provincializing Europe follows directly from my involvement in this project' (p. 15). 'Subaltern Studies and Postcolonial Historiography', Nepantla 1:1 (2000), pp. 9–32, read in the Project MUSE PDF: he reads 'the work of the historian Ranajit Guha in the period when he acted as the founding editor', 'the founding texts of the project' (p. 11), to show 'a radical departure from English Marxist historiographical traditions' (p. 11); 'In rejecting the category “pre-political”, however, Guha insists on the specific differences in the histories of power in colonial India and in Europe. This gesture is radical in that it fundamentally pluralizes the history of power in global modernity and separates it from any universal history of capital' (p. 19). He also reads a 'tension between a familiar narrative of capital and a more radical understanding of it' within Elementary Aspects, which 'sometimes does speak within' a Marxist transition narrative of 'lingering feudalism' (p. 18). Earlier, documented working ties: Guha's 1982 statement thanks 'Dipesh Chakrabarty' among those who commented on an earlier version (Selected Subaltern Studies reprint, p. 37, n. 1), and the Elementary Aspects preface names him among the colleagues of the collective who read the final draft. Criticism of the trajectory: Sarkar (1997, pp. 84–85) calls the path Chakrabarty outlined 'debilitating in both academic and political terms' (recorded on edge_915). This is an influence edge, not a claim that Chakrabarty's argument is Guha's; the Nepantla essay is Chakrabarty's own account of the project.

edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Not proposed as a person edge. The 1982 critique targets the historiography of Indian nationalism, and the atlas maps that position on nationaltradition, where he has a critic roster row and the national_exclusions strand (edge 2). The anticolonial entry's roster (James, Williams, Fanon, Rodney, Césaire, Cabral, Naoroji) is not his target, and no checked text engages them. 'The Prose of Counter-Insurgency' does criticise radical Indian histories of the Santal hool that place it in 'a protracted campaign for freedom and socialism' (pp. 32–33, 39), but those authors (Natarajan, Rasul, Ray) have no atlas rows. edge_114 (subaltern → anticolonial) stays as a collective edge; an optional relabel removing his name is proposed below.

Not proposed. The claim that his founding texts have 'a necessarily postcolonial outlook' is Chakrabarty's later reading (Nepantla, 2000, p. 10), not Guha's in-period position. Said's 1988 foreword calls the 1982 statement 'intellectually insurrectionary' (quoted by Chakrabarty, p. 24; foreword unread) and belongs with the Said entry. edge_115 (subaltern → post) carries the collective contribution.

edges_considered_not_proposed.pair: marx → ranajit_guha / ep_thompson → ranajit_guha (history from below)
edges_considered_not_proposed.reason: Not drawn as separate influence arrows. Sarkar's participant account (1997, p. 83) names British Marxian social history as 'probably the most significant' influence and Thompson's 'plebeian' as a model for 'subaltern', and Elementary Aspects uses Whigs and Hunters (pp. 89–90) and Marx (p. 12, quoting MECW VI 504). But Guha's own checked texts also criticise Hobsbawm (edge 4), Thompson's rule of law (edge 5) and radical historiography 'even when that is done, regrettably, in the name of Marxism' (Prose, p. 39). edge_083 (marx → subaltern) already records the contested reception for the collective; the two critique edges carry Guha's own position. A reviewer could add ep_thompson → ranajit_guha (influence) on the strength of Sarkar p. 83 and EAP pp. 89–90 if the atlas wants both directions.

Not proposed. The 1989 attack on 'neo-colonialist historiography' (pp. 291–292, 299–303) targets the Cambridge historians of India (Seal, Gallagher, Washbrook), not Skinner's and Pocock's Cambridge School of intellectual history mapped as context. No atlas entry holds the Cambridge historians of India; Namier, whose method they are often said to share, is on political, but no checked Guha text names him.

Not proposed. The 1989 essay quotes Hayden White on 'an irreducible ideological component in every historical account of reality' (pp. 214–215) in a single passage; one supporting quotation is not evidence of influence.

Belongs with the Spivak person entry, if drafted; she has no node yet. Her 1985 essay (pp. 330–363, read) is a reading 'from within but against the grain' (p. 341) that recasts the project rather than rejecting it. It is recorded on edge 1 and in the node text.

Not proposed, and not to be confused: edge_699 (post → environment) concerns Ramachandra Guha's deep-ecology argument. O'Hanlon (1988, p. 85) discusses Ramachandra Guha's Subaltern Studies IV essay on Kumaun forest protest; that is his work, not Ranajit Guha's.

edge_604.reason: edge_604 (subaltern → nationaltradition, critique) is labelled 'Guha: two forms of historical elitism'. Edge 2 carries that argument from the person entry, so two arrows would tell the same story (precedents: edge_886 in 1.129, edge_063 in 1.130, edge_720 in 1.131, edge_742 in 1.132). The relabel gives the collective's critique, extended by Chatterjee from nationalist historiography to nationalist thought.

current.relationship: Guha challenges colonialist and bourgeois-nationalist elitism in Indian historiography
current.map_label: Guha: two forms of historical elitism

proposed.relationship: Subaltern Studies criticises elite accounts of Indian nationalism and extends the critique from nationalist historiography to nationalist thought (1982–93)
proposed.map_label: Subaltern critiques of nationalist history and thought, 1982–93
proposed.evidence_note: Guha's 1982 statement (read) opened the collective's critique; his own contribution is the separate edge from his person entry. Sarkar (1997, pp. 91–92, read), a former member, traces how Partha Chatterjee's Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986) carried the critique to the colonized intelligentsia's 'derivative discourses', and objects that 'A project that had started with a trenchant attack on elite nationalist historiography had now chosen as its hero the principal iconic figure of official Indian nationalism' (p. 92). Later reading, labelled: Chakrabarty (2000, p. 25) writes that Chatterjee's book 'extended Guha's criticisms of nationalist historiography into a full-blown, brilliant critique of nationalist thought itself'. The arrow does not claim a denial of all national histories.

edge_604.alternative: Leave edge_604 unchanged if reviewers read it as the subaltern entry's critique with Guha as its example.

edge_357.reason: edge_357 (subaltern → political, contribution) is labelled 'Guha: insurgent peasants as political actors' and rests only on guha_elementary. Edge 3 carries that argument from the person entry. The relabel keeps the collective contribution, documented in Sarkar's account of the early volumes, with Bayly's in-period criticism.

current.relationship: Guha treats colonial peasant insurgency as deliberate political action and consciousness
current.map_label: Guha: insurgent peasants as political actors

proposed.relationship: Subaltern Studies essays treat peasant, tribal and worker action under colonial rule as politics with its own forms, and are criticised for overstating its autonomy (1982–88)
proposed.evidence_note: Sarkar (1997, pp. 86–87, read against the page images) lists early work that explored 'popular or subaltern autonomy in action, consciousness and culture': Hardiman on the peasant nationalists of Gujarat, Pandey on Congress organization and peasant militancy, Amin on rumours of Gandhi, studies of 'tribal movements and cults' and of Bengal labour. Bayly (1988; Verso reprint pp. 116–126, read) finds the essays' empirical work strong but holds that 'their concern to emphasize peasant autonomy seems to have deflected them from moving towards a “total history”' (p. 121) and that 'Simply to stress that autonomy ... is not very helpful in any attempt to specify the nature of historical change' (p. 126). O'Hanlon (1988; reprint pp. 85–86) criticises the 'literal interpretation of subaltern autonomy' in several contributions (Henningham, Ramachandra Guha, Dasgupta) while setting Ranajit Guha's book apart (p. 85). Ranajit Guha's own argument is the separate edge from his person entry.

edge_357.alternative: Leave edge_357 unchanged if reviewers prefer to keep the subaltern entry's political edge tied to Elementary Aspects.

edge_114.reason: edge_114 (subaltern → anticolonial, critique) is labelled 'Guha: popular politics beyond elite leadership'. With a Guha person entry, his name on a group edge invites duplication; his own critique is edge 2 (to nationaltradition). Sarkar documents a collective modification of the historiography of anti-colonial nationalism, which the edge can carry without his name.

current.relationship: Guha challenges elite accounts of anticolonial nationalism with popular political initiatives
current.map_label: Guha: popular politics beyond elite leadership

proposed.relationship: Subaltern Studies modifies the historiography of anti-colonial nationalism through an emphasis on 'pressures from below' and popular initiative beyond elite leadership (1982–88)
proposed.evidence_note: Sarkar (1997, p. 86, read against the page image): the group's publications 'helped to significantly modify the historiography of anticolonial nationalism through a common initial emphasis on “pressures from below”', citing Hardiman, Pandey and Amin; it had been argued 'with considerable justice by Guha and other contributors' that anti-colonial movements had been explained 'far too often' by economic pressures and mobilization from the top (p. 85). He also notes that the critique of nationalist leaders restraining mass initiative 'had been quite common in some kinds of Marxist writing, most notably in R. P. Dutt's India Today' (p. 86, n. 8). The challenge concerns elite nationalist historiography, not every liberation movement or anti-colonial history.

edge_114.alternative: Leave edge_114 unchanged; it is a different target from edge 2 and may be read as the collective's edge with Guha as its example.

new_sources.title: Ranajit Guha, “The Prose of Counter-Insurgency”, in Ranajit Guha, ed., Subaltern Studies II: Writings on South Asian History and Society (Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1983), 1–42.
new_sources.citation: Ranajit Guha, “The Prose of Counter-Insurgency”, Subaltern Studies II (Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1983), pp. 1–42; reprinted in Selected Subaltern Studies (1988).

verification.note: Read in full in a 24-image scan (two pages per image) on the Internet Archive (file RanajitGuhaart--theProseOfCounter-insurgency_text.pdf), with the volume's title page (Subaltern Studies II, Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1983) and imprint '© Oxford University Press 1983'; OCR'd locally at 300 dpi. Running heads give pp. 1–42 (text pp. 1–40, appendix pp. 40–42). Passages used: insurgency 'a motivated and conscious undertaking' and the rebel not taken 'as an entity whose will and reason constituted the praxis called rebellion' (p. 2); 'Cause is made to stand in as a phantom surrogate for Reason'; primary, secondary and tertiary discourse (p. 3); tertiary discourse 'excludes the rebel as the conscious subject of his own history and incorporates the latter as only a contingent element in another history with another subject'; historiography should 'stop pretending that it can fully grasp a past consciousness and reconstitute it' (p. 33); bourgeois-nationalist 'grotesqueries' (p. 38); 'even when that is done, regrettably, in the name of Marxism' (p. 39); radical tertiary discourse 'distanced itself from the prose of counter-insurgency only by a declaration of sentiment so far' (p. 40). The Internet Archive item title says 'Subaltern Studies 3', but the scanned title page is volume II.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period (1983) essay: the three discourses on peasant insurgency and the critique of colonialist, nationalist and radical historiography.

new_sources.title: Ranajit Guha, “Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography”, in Ranajit Guha, ed., Subaltern Studies VI: Writings on South Asian History and Society (Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1989), 210–309.
new_sources.citation: Ranajit Guha, “Dominance without Hegemony and Its Historiography”, Subaltern Studies VI (Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1989), pp. 210–309; revised as Dominance without Hegemony: History and Power in Colonial India (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1997).

verification.note: Read in the Digital Library of India scan of Subaltern Studies VI on the Internet Archive (item dli.bengal.10689.12813; metadata: 1989, Oxford University Press, Delhi), through its OCR text with running heads: pp. 210–215, 227–233, 276–277, 291–292 and 299–303; the rest is unread. Passages used: 'one Indian battle that Britain never won' (p. 210); British rule set up 'as a rule of property' (p. 211); 'a game for two to play' and the liberal 'fundamental agreement' of the two bourgeoisies (p. 212); Hayden White quoted (pp. 214–215); dominance 'quite erroneously been endowed with hegemony' (p. 228); Dominance (D), Subordination (S), Coercion (C), Persuasion (P), Collaboration and Resistance (R) (p. 229); hegemony as D in which 'Persuasion (P) outweighs Coercion (C)', avoiding 'the Gramscian juxtaposition of domination and hegemony' (p. 231); 'the absurdity of the idea of an uncoercive state' (p. 232); Thompson and the rule of law as 'a cultural achievement of universal significance' (pp. 276–277; notes cite Whigs and Hunters, 1975, p. 265); 'neo-colonialist historiography' whose subject 'is the Empire' (p. 292); 'a kind of academic confidence trick' (p. 300). The 1997 Harvard book was not seen: Open Library work OL1932410W gives Harvard University Press, 1997; Spivak's 'The New Subaltern' (Verso, 2000, n. 3) quotes the hegemony definition from its p. 23 ('As used in this work').

new_sources.scope_note: In-period (1989) essay later revised as the 1997 book: hegemony, the colonial state and colonialist and nationalist historiography.

Scott's foreword to the 1999 Duke printing of Elementary Aspects (p. xiii, read) recommends 'his fine earlier work', A Rule of Property for Bengal (Duke, 1996; Paris: Mouton, 1963). new_sources.title: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, “Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography”, in Ranajit Guha, ed., Subaltern Studies IV: Writings on South Asian History and Society (Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985), 330–363.
new_sources.citation: Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, “Subaltern Studies: Deconstructing Historiography”, Subaltern Studies IV (Delhi: Oxford University Press, 1985), pp. 330–363; reprinted in Selected Subaltern Studies (1988), pp. 3–32.

verification.note: Read in the Digital Library of India scan of Subaltern Studies IV on the Internet Archive (item dli.bengal.10689.12766; metadata 1985, Oxford University Press, Delhi), through its OCR text with running heads; the essay opens on p. 330 under the heading 'Discussion'. Pages used: 'offers a theory of change' (p. 330); 'closer to deconstruction' (p. 332); not 'consonant with a desire to find a consciousness (here of the subaltern) in a positive and pure state' (p. 333); 'from within but against the grain' and the quotation of Elementary Aspects p. 15 (p. 341); 'a strategic use of positivist essentialism in a scrupulously visible political interest' (p. 342); 'the dangerous hook of claiming to establish the truth-knowledge of the subaltern'; 'scrupulous in its consideration towards women' but overlooking 'the concept-metaphor woman' (p. 356); woman 'as a structural rather than marginal issue' (p. 361). Chakrabarty (2000, p. 24) dates the essay to the sixth volume, 1986; the scanned volume is IV (1985). The 1988 reprint pagination (pp. 3–32) is from standard citations and was not checked.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period (1985) reading of the Subaltern Studies project, including Guha's Elementary Aspects, by a later co-editor: a critique from within.

new_sources.title: Rosalind O'Hanlon, “Recovering the Subject: Subaltern Studies and Histories of Resistance in Colonial South Asia”, Modern Asian Studies 22, no. 1 (1988): 189–224.
new_sources.citation: Rosalind O'Hanlon, “Recovering the Subject: Subaltern Studies and Histories of Resistance in Colonial South Asia”, Modern Asian Studies 22:1 (1988): 189–224; reprinted in Vinayak Chaturvedi, ed., Mapping Subaltern Studies and the Postcolonial (London: Verso, 2000), 72–115.

verification.note: Read in the Verso reprint (Mapping Subaltern Studies and the Postcolonial, 2000, pp. 72–115; Internet Archive item chaturvedi-v.-mapping-subaltern-studies-and-the-postcolonial, text layer), pp. 72–89, 102, 108–109 and notes; page numbers cited are the reprint's. OpenAlex W2162225742 and the DOI give Modern Asian Studies 22:1, pp. 189–224; the original pagination was not seen. Passages used: 'the classic figure of Western humanism' readmitted 'in the figure of the subaltern himself' (p. 74); 'I want to distinguish Ranajit Guha's work in the book Elementary Aspects' from literal readings of autonomy (p. 85); Dipankar Gupta's 'ethnicised history' and the 'culturological' style 'carried to an extreme' in Elementary Aspects (p. 86); 'Guha's drive to posit an originary autonomy' (p. 87); the subject-agent pursued 'with great deliberation and purposefulness' (p. 88); 'humanism's unitary subject-agent in its most extreme form' (p. 89); no 'theory of domination as hegemony', and agreement with Suneet Chopra and Javeed Alam that the series 'has not turned out to be a Gramscian project at all' (p. 102); n. 6 identifies Alam's 'critical review article, written from a Marxist perspective', Social Scientist no. 117 (February 1983), unread.

new_sources.scope_note: In-period (1988) critique of the Subaltern Studies project and Guha's Elementary Aspects.

new_sources.title: C. A. Bayly, “Rallying Around the Subaltern”, Journal of Peasant Studies 16, no. 1 (1988): 110–120.
new_sources.citation: C. A. Bayly, “Rallying Around the Subaltern”, Journal of Peasant Studies 16:1 (1988): 110–120; reprinted in Chaturvedi, ed., Mapping Subaltern Studies and the Postcolonial (Verso, 2000), 116–126.

verification.note: Read in full in the Verso reprint (2000, pp. 116–126), whose page numbers are cited; the reprint opens 'Rereading Subaltern Studies, volumes I to IV now [1988]'. OpenAlex W1965609660 and the DOI give Journal of Peasant Studies 16:1, pp. 110–120. Bayly reviews volumes I–IV and sets Elementary Aspects aside ('is not at issue here', p. 117). Passages used: the Subalterns 'acted mainly as a catalyst' (p. 116); 'theory as the elite historians used it, as a piquant garnish for footnotes' (pp. 117–118); Guha's approach 'seems sometimes to postulate the existence of an unchanging peasantry and unified peasant consciousness defined by struggle with colonialism' (p. 121); emphasis on autonomy deflected a 'total history' (p. 121); 'every subaltern was an elite to someone lower than him'; stressing autonomy 'is not very helpful in any attempt to specify the nature of historical change' (p. 126).

new_sources.scope_note: In-period (1988) review of Subaltern Studies I–IV by a historian of India outside the collective.

new_sources.title: Dipesh Chakrabarty, “Subaltern Studies and Postcolonial Historiography”, Nepantla: Views from South 1, no. 1 (2000): 9–32.
new_sources.citation: Dipesh Chakrabarty, “Subaltern Studies and Postcolonial Historiography”, Nepantla: Views from South 1:1 (2000): 9–32.

Passages used: Guha 'the inspiration behind it'; he retired from the editorial collective in 1988 (p. 9); 'a necessarily postcolonial outlook' (p. 10); 'the founding editor', 'the founding texts of the project' (p. 11); the series began 'as a critique of two contending schools of history: the Cambridge school and that of the nationalist historians' (p. 14); the redefinition of 'the political' as 'the critical theoretical break' (p. 15); Hobsbawm (1978, 2) quoted with 'express their aspirations about the world' (p. 16); the 'tension' within Elementary Aspects (p. 18); the rejection of the 'pre-political' 'fundamentally pluralizes the history of power in global modernity' (p. 19); Spivak and O'Hanlon on gender and the subject (p. 24); Chatterjee 'extended Guha's criticisms of nationalist historiography' (p. 25). A member's account of the project; cited as a labelled reading and, for edge 7, as Chakrabarty's own statement of his debt.

guha_historiography.note: Re-read in full for the Guha person entry, including the Preface (Selected Subaltern Studies reprint pp. 35–36; dated Canberra, August 1981). Quoted: 'rectify the elitist bias'; 'of inferior rank'; subordination 'expressed in terms of class, caste, age, gender and office'; Gramsci's six-point project and 'subaltern groups are always subject to the activity of ruling groups, even when they rebel and rise up' (p. 35); 'colonialist elitism and bourgeois-nationalist elitism' (p. 37); 'spiritual biography of the Indian elite' and 'not without its uses' (p. 38); 'the contribution made by the people on their own' (p. 39); 'the politics of the people', 'an autonomous domain', 'As modern as indigenous elite politics' (p. 40); 'the failure of the Indian bourgeoisie to speak for the nation' (p. 41); 'a great deal of overlap' (p. 42); 'Let a hundred flowers blossom'; 'We claim no more than to try and indicate an orientation' (p. 43); the note on terms (p. 44). Note 1 thanks Gautam Bhadra, Dipesh Chakrabarty and Raghabendra Chattopadhyay. Reprint pages; Subaltern Studies I pagination (pp. 1–8) is cited by Sarkar and O'Hanlon.

guha_elementary.note: Primary text now read for the Guha person entry. Introduction pp. 1–17 OCR'd at 300 dpi from a scan of the Duke University Press 1999 printing (foreword by James C. Scott) hosted by Berhampore Girls' College; preface dated Canberra, January 1983; the text keeps the 1983 Oxford pagination, checked against the Digital Library of India scan of the Delhi 1983 edition (Internet Archive dli.bengal.10689.12632; imprint 'First published 1983, Second impression 1986'). Quoted: 'Insurgency was thus the necessary antithesis of colonialism' (p. 2); 'a discourse of power'; the peasant 'denied recognition as a subject of history' (p. 3); 'a consciousness'; spontaneity 'elitist as well as erroneous' (p. 4); Gramsci on spontaneity; Hobsbawm's 'pioneering work' and 'pre-political' (p. 5); 'helps little in understanding the experience of colonial India'; 'nothing ... that was not political' (p. 6); 'a composite apparatus of dominance' (p. 8); 'negative and inversive procedure' (p. 9); limits that define 'the quality of that politics' (p. 10); 'inchoate and naive' (p. 11); Gramsci's 'pillars of politics' and 'elementary aspects' (p. 12); 'its sovereignty, its consistency and its logic' (p. 13); reading rebel consciousness in counter-insurgency records (pp. 14–15). Bibliography: Gramsci, Selections (1971); Hobsbawm, Primitive Rebels (Manchester, 1959); Hobsbawm and Rudé, Captain Swing (1969). Pp. 89–90 (Thompson on the Blacks; Hobsbawm's 'social banditry') read in the 1983 edition's text. Scott's foreword: Elementary Aspects 'became, in effect, the founding document' of 'the Subaltern Studies School' (p. ix). The rest of the book is unread.

sarkar_decline.note: Re-read for the Guha person entry: pp. 82–87 and 90–94 OCR'd, pp. 84–87 checked against the page images. Quoted: Guha's 1982 preface and essay 'full of references to “subaltern classes”, evocations of Gramsci' (p. 82); British Marxian social history 'probably the most significant' influence and Guha's 'subaltern' used 'somewhat in the way Thompson deployed the term “plebeian”' (p. 83; n. 3: Elementary Aspects 'frequently cited Thompson with approval', to Whigs and Hunters and Albion's Fatal Tree); the early volumes 'largely ignored in the West' (p. 84; n. 4 names O'Hanlon 1988 as Modern Asian Studies' first engagement); 'argued with considerable justice by Guha and other contributors' (p. 85; n. 7: 'A more explicit critique of orthodox Marxist historiography was made by Guha' in 'The Prose of Counterinsurgency'); 'over-flamboyant' paradigm claims and the group's modification of 'the historiography of anticolonial nationalism' (p. 86); 'Guha's attempt to use some of the language and methods of Lévi-Straussian structuralism' (p. 87); Chatterjee's 'derivative discourses' (p. 91); 'an unnoticed drift implicit even in Guha's initial formulation' (p. 92); Guha's 'Chandra's Death' as a 'seldom-referred-to' alternative (pp. 93–94).

gramsci.note: Checked for the Guha person entry: 'Subaltern groups are always subject to the activity of ruling groups, even when they rebel and rise up' ('Notes on Italian History', p. 55), the sentence Guha's 1982 preface quotes; and 'Elements of Politics', p. 144: the 'first elements' which, repeated, 'become the pillars of politics and of any collective action whatsoever', which Elementary Aspects cites (Gramsci: 144).
